questions.prompt: In an NMOS transistor, what are the source and drain?
options: Heavily doped n+ regions on either side of the gate in a p-type body
p+ regions in an n-type body
Metal contacts on the oxide
Two gates on either side of the channel
questions.explanation: The NMOS is a MOS capacitor (p body) with n+ regions added at each end of the gate; they supply and collect the inversion electrons (reader Sec. 8.2).

questions.prompt: Which dimension is the channel length \(L\)?
options: The width of the gate perpendicular to current flow
The distance from source to drain under the gate
The thickness of the gate oxide
The depth of the source and drain regions
questions.explanation: Current flows from drain to source along \(L\); \(W\) is the perpendicular width. The current scales with \(W/L\).

questions.prompt: In a CMOS process on a p-type substrate, where is the PMOS built?
options: Directly in the p substrate, with p+ source and drain
On top of the field oxide
Inside an n-well, with p+ source and drain
In a separate wafer bonded on top
questions.explanation: A PMOS needs an n-type body, so an n-well is implanted into the p substrate; NMOS devices sit directly in the substrate (reader Sec. 8.2.4).

questions.prompt: Why is the body of an NMOS normally tied to the lowest supply (ground)?
options: To turn the channel on
To set the oxide capacitance
To cancel the gate leakage
So the source/drain-to-body junctions are never forward biased
questions.explanation: Source and drain are n+ regions in the p body: two diodes. Keeping the body at the lowest potential keeps them reverse biased.

questions.prompt: A designer needs \(W/L = 25\) with the minimum length \(L = 0.13\ \mu\mathrm{m}\). What width (in µm) is required?
questions.explanation: \(W = (W/L)\cdot L = 25 \times 0.13 = 3.25\ \mu\mathrm{m}\). Designers set \(L\) at the minimum for speed and choose \(W\) for current.

questions.prompt: What does the circle on a PMOS gate symbol indicate?
options: The device turns on when the gate is pulled low relative to the source
The gate is floating
The device is a depletion-mode NMOS
The body is tied to the drain
questions.explanation: Like a logic inversion bubble: a PMOS conducts for \(V_{GS}\) sufficiently negative (\(V_{SG} > |V_{Tp}|\)).

questions.prompt: Electrically, what distinguishes the source from the drain of a symmetric NMOS?
options: The source is always the region nearer the body contact
Nothing structural; the source is whichever n+ region is at the lower voltage
The drain is always more heavily doped
The source is defined by the symbol arrow only
questions.explanation: The layout is symmetric. Carriers (electrons) come from the lower-potential end, which we call the source.

questions.prompt: Two transistors have \(L = 0.5\ \mu\mathrm{m}\); M1 has \(W = 4\ \mu\mathrm{m}\), M2 has \(W = 10\ \mu\mathrm{m}\). At the same bias, what is the ratio \(I_{D2}/I_{D1}\)?
questions.explanation: The drain current is proportional to \(W/L\): \(10/4 = 2.5\).

questions.prompt: Preview of NMOS regions: with \(V_{GS}\) below threshold, what does the drain current look like (ideally)?
options: A resistor-like current set by \(R_\square\)
A large current limited only by the drain resistance
Essentially zero: no inversion channel connects source and drain
Reverse diode current that grows with \(V_{GS}\)
questions.explanation: Without inversion, source and drain are two back-to-back junctions; the device is in cut-off.

questions.prompt: Preview of the square law: an NMOS has \(\mu_nC_{ox} = 250\ \mu\mathrm{A/V^2}\), \(W/L = 10\) and is in saturation with \(V_{ov} = 0.3\ \mathrm{V}\). Using \(I_D = \tfrac12\mu_nC_{ox}\tfrac WL V_{ov}^2\), find \(I_D\) in µA.
Preview of PMOS: why are PMOS devices usually drawn wider than NMOS devices for equal current?
options: The n-well has higher capacitance
PMOS oxides are thicker
PMOS thresholds are always larger
Hole mobility is lower than electron mobility
questions.explanation: \(\mu_p\) is roughly a third to half of \(\mu_n\), so a PMOS needs larger \(W/L\) to carry the same current.
